summary: This document describes a BGP mechanism that reduces the harm done to routing when BGP restarts. It defines an End-of-RIB marker, a Graceful Restart capability for announcing the ability to preserve forwarding state, and procedures to keep routing information across a TCP session reset. It updates RFC 4271 and was later updated by RFC 8538.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4724 defines a way for BGP routers to keep using saved routes while a neighbor restarts and rebuilds its routing information. It can reduce disruption, but routers must remove saved routes when the restart does not recover as expected. RFC 8538 later updated this specification.

questions: what happens to bgp routes when a router restarts
subtitle: Keeps BGP routes useful while a router restores its routing session.

tldr.problem: When BGP restarts, peers can withdraw routes and recalculate paths, causing temporary traffic loops or black holes.
tldr.mechanism: Graceful Restart lets a peer keep forwarding with retained routes while the restarted router rebuilds its session and sends fresh updates. An End-of-RIB marker signals that the initial update is complete.
tldr.outcome: It can reduce routing disruption during a restart, but retained forwarding state must still be valid. RFC 4724 is updated by RFC 8538.

today: RFC 4724 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271 and is itself updated by RFC 8538.

sections.title: Why BGP Restarts Disrupt Routing
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) shares routes between routers. When a router's BGP process restarts, its peers can see the session go down and up, recalculate routes, and send many updates.

This routing flap can briefly create forwarding black holes or loops and consume router resources. Graceful Restart aims to reduce these effects by keeping forwarding state while the BGP session is restored.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP restart can make nearby routers withdraw and recalculate routes, even when the restarting router can still forward packets. This specification lets them keep routes temporarily while the BGP conversation is restored.

sections.title: The End-of-RIB Marker
sections.content:
An End-of-RIB marker is an UPDATE message with no reachable routes and no withdrawn routes. For IPv4 unicast it is the minimum-length UPDATE; for other address families it carries an empty MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute.

A speaker sends the marker after completing its initial routing update for an address family, including when it has no routes to send. Its peer can use the marker to know that the initial update is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The End-of-RIB marker tells a peer that the initial route update for an address family is finished. It is sent even when there are no routes to report.

sections.title: The Graceful Restart Capability
sections.content:
A BGP speaker advertises the Graceful Restart capability to signal support for the procedures. Capability code 64 carries restart flags, a restart time in seconds, and optional address-family entries.

The Restart State flag indicates that the speaker has restarted. A per-address-family Forwarding State flag says whether forwarding state was preserved. A capability without address-family entries can still indicate support for the receiving-speaker procedures and intent to send End-of-RIB markers.
sections.plainLanguage: The capability tells a peer whether the router restarted and whether it kept forwarding routes for each address family. The peer uses this information to decide whether saved routes can be kept temporarily.

sections.title: How Peers Restore Routes
sections.content:
After restarting, a speaker retains and marks its old forwarding routes as stale when possible. It delays route selection until it receives End-of-RIB markers from relevant peers or its selection-deferral timer expires, then installs updated routes and sends its initial updates.

A receiving speaker keeps the restarting peer's routes as stale and continues forwarding with them. It removes stale routes if the session does not return within the advertised Restart Time, if the restarted speaker does not confirm preserved forwarding state, or when the peer's End-of-RIB marker shows that fresh updates are complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The restarted router rebuilds its routes while its peer temporarily keeps the old routes for forwarding. Fresh updates replace those routes, and the End-of-RIB marker tells the peer when to remove any old routes still left.

sections.title: Limits and Deployment Risks
sections.content:
Graceful Restart reduces some routing flaps, but it cannot guarantee that retained forwarding state remains usable. A restart that loses forwarding state, or a deployment where only some internal BGP speakers support the mechanism, can still expose the network to temporary loops or black holes.

The RFC says operators may need to tune restart and deferral timers. It also notes that tightly coupled BGP and interior gateway protocol restarts can reduce the benefit when the interior protocol lacks a similar restart mechanism. The security model remains that of BGP; authenticated BGP sessions are relevant to protection against false connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping old routes helps only while the router can still forward with them. A restart can still cause loops or black holes, so the timers and the rest of the network's behavior matter.
